title: Transport in multilayer graphene: resistance from stacking faults
authors: C. M. Wilson, R. Ganesh, K. V. Samokhin
abstract: Multilayer graphene exhibits rich possibilities for stacking. While natural bulk graphite predominantly occurs in the Bernal structure, where layers are stacked in an $-ABAB-$ pattern, rhombohedral stacking has sprung to prominence recently. It is well known that Bernal graphite exhibits anisotropic transport, with high resistance to currents along the stacking axis. Careful experiments using pillar geometries have measured out-of-plane resistance, attributing it to stacking faults where planes slip out of the nominal $ABAB$ sequence. The observed resistance shows anomalously large, non-Gaussian, sample-to-sample variations. In this article, we build a theoretical framework to calculate $c$-axis resistance of graphene stacks with an arbitrary stacking arrangement. Our approach builds on the idea that, regardless of stacking sequence, we have in-plane translational symmetry. With in-plane momentum as a good quantum number, $c$-axis transport reduces to an effectively one-dimensional problem that can be addressed using the Landauer paradigm. We calculate the resistances of a variety of simple stacking faults in both Bernal and rhombohedral systems. We also calculate the resistance of a rhombohedral 'slab' embedded between Bernal leads. Remarkably, despite both Bernal and rhombohedral graphite being metallic, the system exhibits insulating behaviour. We attribute this to Fermi surface mismatch. We next calculate the resistance of a multilayer sample with stacking disorder. Resistance is non-self-averaging, akin to a one-dimensional wire where disorder has a strong localizing effect. The median resistance grows exponentially with stack size, indicating insulating character driven by localization. Our results demonstrate that transport measurements on mesoscopic graphitic pillars serve as signatures of stacking faults, and in particular, probe localization-driven physics.
summary: This paper develops a theoretical framework to calculate the electrical resistance across multilayer graphene stacks, paying special attention to the role of stacking faults. Using the Landauer formalism, the authors show that even metallic graphite structures can exhibit insulating behavior due to Fermi surface mismatch and that disorder leads to strong localization. The work demonstrates that transport measurements are powerful probes of localization-driven physics in graphitic materials.
main_problem: To theoretically calculate the c-axis resistance of multilayer graphene stacks, focusing on how stacking faults and disorder affect transport.
main_result: The system exhibits insulating behavior due to Fermi surface mismatch, and the resistance in disordered samples is non-self-averaging, growing exponentially with stack size due to localization.
method: The study employs the Landauer formalism combined with Green's function techniques to reduce the c-axis transport to an effectively one-dimensional problem.
model_or_system: The system is multilayer graphene, modeled using a minimal tight-binding Hamiltonian that accounts for Bernal (ABAB) and rhombohedral (ABC) stacking arrangements.
key_observables: c-axis resistance, transmission probability T(E), and the exponential growth of median resistance with stack size.
important_parameters: Hopping parameters (gamma_0, gamma_1), Fermi energy (pinned at zero), and stack size (N).
main_assumptions: Translational symmetry is assumed in the lateral (x, y) directions, allowing in-plane momentum k to be a good quantum number.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the local atomic environment and the general transport setup (Lead-Device-Lead), while equations detail the calculation of self-energies and transmission.
paper_structure: The paper develops a theoretical framework using Green's functions to calculate resistance for various stacking faults, analyzes the resulting localization physics, and compares results for Bernal and rhombohedral structures.
why_interesting: The strong localization effects observed in the transport measurements provide a concrete, solid-state realization of Anderson localization physics, which is a key topic in disordered systems.
